h1: Texas HOA Lien or Foreclosure Threat Response Demand Letter
metaTitle: Texas HOA Lien & Foreclosure Demand Letter Tool
metaDescription: Generate a Texas HOA lien or foreclosure threat response demand letter. Protect your home under Chapter 209 of the Texas Property Code with a strong, statute-backed reply.
statuteCitation: Texas Property Code Chapter 209 (Texas Residential Property Owners Protection Act)
deadline: 30 days to cure after notice; HOA must wait 180 days after court order before foreclosure sale
penalty: Right to redemption within 180 days, judicial foreclosure required, plus actual damages and attorney's fees for violations
introParagraph: If you've received a lien notice or foreclosure threat from your Texas HOA, you have stronger legal protections than most homeowners realize. Texas Property Code Chapter 209, known as the Texas Residential Property Owners Protection Act, gives homeowners specific rights before an HOA can place a lien or foreclose on a home. The HOA must follow strict notice rules, offer payment plans, and obtain a court order before any foreclosure sale. A properly drafted demand letter that cites Chapter 209 can stop unlawful collection tactics, force the HOA to accept a payment plan, and preserve your right to redemption. Acting quickly and in writing creates a paper trail that courts and judges respect.
lawExplanation: Texas Property Code Chapter 209 governs how homeowner associations in subdivisions may collect assessments, file liens, and pursue foreclosure. Before an HOA can foreclose, it must send the homeowner a written notice of delinquency by certified mail specifying the amount owed and giving at least 30 days to cure. The notice must also describe the options the owner has to avoid collection, including any payment plan, and Section 209.0062 requires an association of more than 14 lots to adopt reasonable guidelines for an alternative payment schedule with a minimum term of three months. Section 209.009 prohibits foreclosure of the assessment lien if the debt consists solely of fines, attorney's fees associated solely with fines, or certain amounts added to the account as assessments under Sections 209.005(i) or 209.0057(b-4). Section 209.0091 requires the association, before seeking a foreclosure order, to give certified-mail notice of the delinquency to inferior deed-of-trust lienholders and an opportunity to cure before the 61st day after the notice is mailed; separately, Section 209.0064 bars charging you a collection agent's fees unless the association first sends certified-mail notice giving at least 45 days to cure. Section 209.0092 provides that an association may not foreclose an assessment lien unless it first obtains a court order in an expedited foreclosure proceeding under rules adopted by the Texas Supreme Court (the owner can waive this in writing, and other exceptions apply). Section 209.011 allows the owner or a lienholder of record to redeem the property not later than the 180th day after the association mails written notice of the sale, by paying the amounts due, interest, and the association's foreclosure costs. Section 209.0064 limits when an owner can be charged a collection agent's fees, and Section 209.007 gives owners the right to a hearing before the HOA board on a violation notice. Homeowners who prove the HOA violated Chapter 209 can recover actual damages, court costs, and reasonable attorney's fees under Section 209.008. Many disputes also involve improperly itemized fees, unauthorized late charges, or fines mischaracterized as assessments, all of which can defeat a foreclosure attempt.
letterStrategy: A demand letter responding to an HOA lien or foreclosure threat in Texas should accomplish several goals at once: stop improper collection activity, demand a full statutory accounting, and preserve every defense available under Chapter 209. Start by identifying yourself, the property, and the lien or foreclosure notice you received. Cite Texas Property Code Sections 209.0062, 209.0091, 209.0092, and 209.011 to remind the HOA that judicial foreclosure is required, that fines cannot be the basis of foreclosure, and that you have redemption rights. Demand an itemized ledger separating regular assessments from fines, late fees, and attorney's fees, because only true assessments support foreclosure. Request a written payment plan under Section 209.0062 if you cannot pay in full, and note that an association of more than 14 lots must have adopted guidelines for one. Invoke your right to a board hearing under Section 209.007 if any underlying violation is disputed. Set a clear deadline—typically 14 to 30 days—for the HOA or its attorney to respond, and warn that continued violations will trigger a claim for actual damages and attorney's fees under Section 209.008. Send the letter by certified mail, return receipt requested, and keep copies of everything. A well-cited letter often causes HOA attorneys to pause foreclosure, accept a payment plan, or correct an inflated ledger because the cost of litigating a Chapter 209 violation outweighs the unpaid balance.
proceduralNotes: Texas HOAs generally must obtain a court order in an expedited foreclosure proceeding before foreclosing an assessment lien (Section 209.0092), and a homeowner with a Chapter 209 defense can raise it in that proceeding or in a separate suit. Justice court (small claims) handles disputes up to $20,000 and can address improper fees, but title and foreclosure matters belong in district court. Debt claims must generally be brought within four years (Texas Civil Practice & Remedies Code Section 16.004). The 180-day redemption period is strict and runs from the date the association mails written notice of the sale (Section 209.011).

faq.q: Can my Texas HOA foreclose on my home without going to court?
faq.a: Generally no. Under Texas Property Code Section 209.0092, an association may not foreclose an assessment lien unless it first obtains a court order in an expedited foreclosure proceeding, unless you agree in writing to waive that requirement or another exception applies. Even if your declaration grants the HOA a power of sale, that power cannot be exercised without a judge's approval. This requirement gives you a chance to raise defenses, dispute the amount owed, and demand a payment plan before losing your home.

faq.q: Can my HOA foreclose just because I owe fines or attorney's fees?
faq.a: Not if that is all you owe. Texas Property Code Section 209.009 prohibits foreclosure of the assessment lien when the debt consists solely of fines or attorney's fees associated solely with fines. The HOA may only foreclose for unpaid regular or special assessments and reasonable assessment-related charges. If your HOA's ledger lumps fines and legal fees into the foreclosure amount, that's a strong defense. Demand an itemized accounting separating assessments from fines, and the foreclosure amount may shrink dramatically or disappear.

faq.q: Do I have a right to a payment plan in Texas?
faq.a: Often. Texas Property Code Section 209.0062 requires an association of more than 14 lots to adopt reasonable guidelines for an alternative payment schedule (minimum term three months), but the association is not required to allow a plan beyond 18 months, after the cure period under Section 209.0064(b)(3), or more than once in any 12-month period. The minimum plan must allow at least three months to pay, and the HOA cannot charge late fees or interest during the plan if you stay current. If your HOA refuses to offer a written payment plan, that refusal may itself violate Chapter 209 and support a claim for damages.

faq.q: How long do I have to redeem my home after an HOA foreclosure sale?
faq.a: Texas Property Code Section 209.011 lets you redeem the property not later than the 180th day after the association mails written notice of the sale to you and the lienholder. To redeem, you must pay the foreclosure sale price, any unpaid assessments accrued after the sale, attorney's fees, costs, and a small statutory premium. The HOA cannot resell or significantly alter the property during this window. This redemption right is one of the strongest homeowner protections in any state.

faq.q: What if my HOA didn't send proper certified-mail notice before threatening foreclosure?
faq.a: Defective notice is a powerful defense. Texas Property Code Sections 209.0064 and 209.0091 require certified-mail notices giving at least 30 days to cure before the account is referred to an attorney, and a separate notice before foreclosure. If the HOA skipped steps, used regular mail, or failed to itemize amounts, you can demand the process restart. Raise the defect in your demand letter and in any Rule 736 proceeding to delay or defeat the foreclosure.
